issues.legal_issue: A pure question of law that requires no investigation of facts may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The respondent raised in the Supreme Court a legal objection that had not been taken in the courts below.
The objection could be decided without investigating facts.
issues.conclusion: The Court permitted the objection to be raised.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law arising on the facts and circumstances of a case may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if deciding it does not require investigation of facts. The Court applied Yaswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, Raja Sri Sailendra Narayan Bhanja Deo v. State of Orissa, Seth Badri Prasad v. Seth Nagarmal, State of U.P. v. Anand Swarup, and T. G. Appanda Mudaliar v. State of Madras.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and pure_question_of_law and not factual_investigation_needed

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The newly raised plea concerns a question of law arising on the case's facts.
predicates.factual_investigation_needed: Deciding the newly raised plea requires further investigation of facts.

issues.definition: When an appeal is before the Supreme Court and a newly raised plea presents a pure legal question that requires no factual investigation, the plea may be permitted.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement cannot by itself displace title acquired under a registered conveyance, but that limitation does not make a suit based on an independent claim of real ownership non-maintainable.
material_facts: The purchaser obtained a registered conveyance in his own name after the court-confirmed sale.
The claimants relied on an unregistered agreement but also pleaded that the property had been acquired in co-ownership and that they were real owners.
The respondent argued that title under the conveyance prevented the claimants from relying on the unregistered agreement.
issues.conclusion: The claimants could not displace the purchaser's title on the basis of the unregistered agreement alone, but the legal objection did not make the suit non-maintainable because their real-ownership claim was not based on that agreement alone.
issues.legal_principle: An unregistered instrument cannot create an interest that the applicable statute requires to be created by a registered instrument; equity cannot override that statutory requirement. The Court referred to G. H. C. Ariff v. Jadunath Mazumdar Bahadur and Maritime Electric Co. Ltd. v. General Dairies Ltd. It distinguished the effect of that principle from the maintainability of a suit pleaded on an independent claim of real ownership.

predicates.suit_claims_real_ownership: The claimant brings a suit asserting that the property was acquired for the claimant's ownership.
predicates.claim_has_basis_beyond_unregistered_agre: The ownership claim rests on grounds beyond the unregistered agreement alone.
predicates.title_under_registered_conveyance: The opposing title-holder acquired title under a registered conveyance.

issues.definition: If a real-ownership suit rests on more than an unregistered agreement despite an opposing registered title, the suit is not dismissed as non-maintainable merely because of that agreement.

issues.legal_issue: The bar on suits alleging that a court-certified purchaser bought on behalf of the claimant does not apply to a sale conducted through a court-appointed receiver without the prescribed execution-sale certificate.
material_facts: The property was sold through a receiver appointed by the court, acting on the court's directions.
The conveyance was executed under the applicable original-side rules.
The purchaser did not receive the certificate prescribed for an execution sale of immovable property.
The respondent argued that the suit was barred because the purchase had allegedly been made on behalf of the claimants.
issues.conclusion: The statutory bar did not apply to the receiver's sale, and the objection was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a suit against a person claiming title under a purchase certified by the court in the prescribed manner when the suit alleges that the purchase was made on behalf of the claimant. Under section 2(16), 'prescribed' means prescribed by rules. The Court held that the relevant certificate is the certificate under Order 21, rule 94, following confirmation under rule 92. A receiver's sale under Order 40, rule 1 is not an execution sale under Order 21 and does not result in that certificate; section 66 therefore does not apply. The Court considered and distinguished Bishun Dayal v. Kesho Prasad.

rule.if: suit_alleges_purchase_for_claimant and sale_by_court_receiver and not prescribed_execution_sale_certificate

predicates.suit_alleges_purchase_for_claimant: A claimant's suit alleges that the purchaser acquired the property on the claimant's behalf.
predicates.sale_by_court_receiver: The property was sold by a receiver appointed by a court under the court's directions.
predicates.prescribed_execution_sale_certificate: The purchaser received the certificate prescribed for a court execution sale.

issues.definition: When a suit alleges a purchase for the claimant but the property was sold through a court-appointed receiver without the prescribed execution-sale certificate, the statutory bar does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Claimants who established that money was advanced in exchange for agreed ownership shares, rather than as a loan, were entitled to those shares subject to payment of their agreed share of expenses, while a claimant who failed to prove contribution was not entitled to a share.
material_facts: The purchaser signed a written agreement providing that the property would be held in equal shares.
Two claimants each paid a substantial sum toward completion of the purchase, and the Court found that the money was not advanced as a loan but in exchange for shares.
Those two claimants did not prove payment of their additional share of expenses and were directed to pay it.
The first claimant did not prove payment of any part of the consideration.
The Court found no prior agreement that the purchaser's bids had been made on behalf of all claimants.
After the Court delivered its judgment, the parties entered a compromise, and the Court directed that the final decree be passed in its terms.
issues.conclusion: On the merits, the two claimants who had advanced money for ownership shares were entitled to separate possession of one-fourth shares each upon payment of their agreed shares of expenses; the first claimant was not entitled to relief. The final decree was directed to be passed in accordance with the parties' subsequent compromise.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the parties' agreement, payments, and conduct to determine whether the money was a loan or was paid in exchange for ownership shares. It concluded that the purchaser accepted the two claimants' payments on the latter basis, and that their relief was subject to payment of their agreed share of expenses. The claimant seeking a share had to prove the facts supporting that claim.

rule.if: appeal_from_dismissal_of_ownership_claim and written_share_agreement and funds_advanced_for_share_not_loan and claimant_failed_to_prove_contribution

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_ownership_claim: The proceeding is an appeal from dismissal of a suit claiming ownership shares in property.
predicates.written_share_agreement: The proposed purchaser signed a written agreement stating that the property would be shared with the claimants.
predicates.funds_advanced_for_share_not_loan: Claimants advanced funds that the court found were given in exchange for ownership shares rather than as a loan.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_contribution: A claimant seeking a share failed to prove payment of the contribution required to support that share.

issues.definition: In an appeal from dismissal of an ownership claim, a written agreement and funds given for shares rather than as a loan support shares for the funding claimants upon payment of agreed expenses, while a claimant who fails to prove the required contribution receives no share.
